difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE - one concept (f(f(n)) = n forces a permutation made only of fixed points and swaps) followed by a routine three-case count (1 + 6 + 3), roughly 1.5 min for a prepared student, with an easy double-counting trap in the two-swap case.
stem: The number of bijections $f(\cdot)$ from the set $S = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ to itself such that $f(f(n)) = n$, for all $n \in S$, is __________ . (Answer in **integer**)

solution.quick: $f(f(n)) = n$ means $f$ is its own inverse (an **involution**), so in cycle notation it consists only of fixed points and 2-cycles (swaps). On 4 elements: no swap (identity) $= 1$, one swap $= \binom{4}{2} = 6$, two disjoint swaps $= 3$. Total $= 1 + 6 + 3 = $ **10**.

steps.title: Translate the condition into cycle structure
steps.body:
A bijection of a finite set to itself is a **permutation**, and every permutation splits into disjoint cycles. If $n$ lies on a cycle of length $L$, then $f^{(m)}(n) = n$ exactly when $L$ divides $m$.

The condition $f(f(n)) = n$ for **every** $n$ therefore requires every cycle length $L$ to divide 2, i.e. $L = 1$ (a fixed point, $f(n) = n$) or $L = 2$ (a swap, $f(a) = b$ and $f(b) = a$). No 3-cycles or 4-cycles are allowed.

(Remark: $f \circ f = \text{id}$ already forces $f$ to be a bijection, since $f$ is then its own inverse, so the word "bijection" adds no extra restriction.)

steps.title: Case 1: zero swaps
steps.body: All four elements are fixed: $f$ is the identity $(1)(2)(3)(4)$. Count $= 1$.

steps.title: Case 2: exactly one swap
steps.body:
Choose the 2 elements to swap; the other two stay fixed. Count $= \binom{4}{2} = 6$:

$(1\,2),\ (1\,3),\ (1\,4),\ (2\,3),\ (2\,4),\ (3\,4)$.

steps.title: Case 3: two disjoint swaps
steps.body:
Split $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ into two unordered pairs. Element 1 can be paired with any of the other 3 elements, and the remaining two elements form the second pair. Count $= 3$:

$(1\,2)(3\,4),\ (1\,3)(2\,4),\ (1\,4)(2\,3)$.

Equivalently $\dfrac{\binom{4}{2}\binom{2}{2}}{2!} = \dfrac{6 \cdot 1}{2} = 3$; divide by $2!$ because the order of the two swaps does not matter.

steps.title: Add the cases and cross-check
steps.body:
$$
1 + 6 + 3 = 10.
$$

Cross-check with the involution recurrence $I(n) = I(n-1) + (n-1)\,I(n-2)$ (element $n$ is either fixed, or swapped with one of the other $n-1$ elements): $I(0) = 1$, $I(1) = 1$, $I(2) = 2$, $I(3) = 2 + 2 \cdot 1 = 4$, $I(4) = 4 + 3 \cdot 2 = 10$. A brute-force check of all $4! = 24$ permutations (see the verification code) also finds exactly 10. This matches the official key (10 to 10).

solution.teaching:
**Permutations and cycles.** A bijection from a finite set to itself is a *permutation*: it rearranges the elements. Start at any element $n$ and keep applying $f$: $n \to f(n) \to f(f(n)) \to \cdots$. Because the set is finite and $f$ is one-to-one, you must eventually return to $n$, tracing a **cycle**. Every permutation breaks up into disjoint cycles; for example, on $\{1,2,3,4\}$ the map $1 \to 3,\ 3 \to 1,\ 2 \to 2,\ 4 \to 4$ is written $(1\,3)(2)(4)$.

**Applying $f$ twice.** Applying $f$ moves each element one step around its cycle, so applying it twice moves each element two steps. An element on a cycle of length $L$ returns home after two steps only if $L$ divides 2. Hence a permutation with $f(f(n)) = n$ for all $n$, called an **involution**, is built only from fixed points (length-1 cycles) and swaps (length-2 cycles).

**Counting involutions.** Organise the count by the number of swaps $k$. Choose $2k$ elements to be swapped in $\binom{n}{2k}$ ways, then pair them up in $\dfrac{(2k)!}{2^k\,k!}$ ways: divide by $2^k$ because each pair is unordered, and by $k!$ because the list of pairs is unordered. So

$$
I(n) = \sum_{k \ge 0} \binom{n}{2k} \frac{(2k)!}{2^k\,k!}.
$$

For $n = 4$: $k = 0$ gives $1$, $k = 1$ gives $6 \cdot 1 = 6$, $k = 2$ gives $1 \cdot \frac{24}{4 \cdot 2} = 3$, so $I(4) = 10$. The sequence $I(n)$ for $n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ runs $1, 1, 2, 4, 10, 26$.

**Connection to this question.** The question describes exactly the involutions of a 4-element set, so the answer is $I(4) = 10$.
solution.shortcut: Use the involution recurrence $I(n) = I(n-1) + (n-1)\,I(n-2)$ with $I(1) = 1$, $I(2) = 2$: $I(3) = 4$, $I(4) = 4 + 3 \cdot 2 = 10$.
solution.commonTrap: Over-counting the two-swap case as $\binom{4}{2}\binom{2}{2} = 6$ (forgetting that the two swaps are unordered), which gives $1 + 6 + 6 = 13$. Other slips are forgetting the identity (answer 9) or counting only the fixed-point-free involutions (answer 3).

answerVerification.method: Author solve (not blind) compared with official key
answerVerification.checkCode:
from itertools import permutations
S = [1, 2, 3, 4]
inv = [p for p in permutations(S) if all(dict(zip(S, p))[dict(zip(S, p))[n]] == n for n in S)]
print(len(inv), inv)          # 10 involutions
I = [1, 1]
for n in range(2, 5): I.append(I[n-1] + (n-1)*I[n-2])   # I(n) = I(n-1) + (n-1) I(n-2)
assert len(inv) == I[4] == 1 + 6 + 3 == 10
answerVerification.notes: f(f(n)) = n forces a permutation made only of fixed points and 2-cycles. Counting by number of swaps gives 1 + 6 + 3 = 10, confirmed by brute force over all 24 permutations and by the recurrence I(n) = I(n-1) + (n-1) I(n-2). Matches official key '10 to 10'.
